title: Longest Subarray Divisible by K with At Most One Negation II
solution: Let P be prefix sums mod k. Subarray [l, r) with sum S is valid iff S ≡ 0 or some i in [l, r) has 2*nums[i] ≡ S (mod k), since negating x changes the sum by -2x. Both conditions depend only on the residues P[l], P[r], so an optimal subarray can always take l = first occurrence of residue c and r = last occurrence of residue d (widening keeps i inside and keeps the sum residue). That leaves at most k×k residue pairs (c, d). Process the first-occurrence positions from right to left while keeping nxt[v] = smallest index i ≥ first[c] with 2*nums[i] mod k = v. Pair (c, d) is valid iff d == c or nxt[(d-c) mod k] < last[d], and it gives length last[d]-first[c]. Total O(n + k^2) time (about 9·10^6 for k ≤ 3000) and O(n + k) memory, versus O(n^2) brute force, which is too slow at n = 10^5.

verified: Python implementation returns 3, 2, 2 on the three samples; also matches an O(n^3) brute force on 3000 random small cases and runs in 0.2s at n=1e5, k=3000

rejected_patterns.reason: Not central. Every key is a prefix residue in [0, k) with k <= 3000, so plain arrays of size k (first[], last[], nxt[]) do the whole job. My reimplementation uses no dictionary and matches brute force. The hard step is reducing the endpoints to first/last occurrences and enumerating k^2 residue pairs, not a hash lookup.

rejected_tags.reason: Same reason: fixed-size arrays indexed by residue replace it, so it would put this problem in front of people looking for real hash-map problems.

notes.solver: Key step: the endpoints reduce to first/last occurrences of prefix residues, so only O(k^2) residue pairs need checking, each with an O(1) next-occurrence lookup for an element with 2x ≡ d-c. k ≤ 3000 is what makes k^2 affordable. An O(n·k) alternative fixes the negated index i and scans residues c, using first-occurrence ≤ i and last-occurrence ≥ i+1 tables; at 3·10^8 operations it is borderline. Rejected sliding-window/two-pointers (validity is not monotone in window size) and binary-search-answer (validity is not monotone in length). Left out brute-force: enumerating residue pairs is not what a brute-force search means.
notes.skeptic: Checked the proposal's O(n + k^2) algorithm independently: it gives 3, 2, 2 on the samples, matches an O(n^3) brute force on 4000 random cases (n <= 12, k <= 12), and runs in 0.7s in Python at n=1e5, k=3000. The widening argument is sound, since moving l to first[c] and r to last[d] keeps l < r, keeps the negated index inside and keeps the sum residue. The proposal's 'borderline O(n*k)' alternative can be amortized to O(n + k^2): keep E0[x] = first prefix with residue x and E1[y] = earliest start with one negation used. For each value v = 2*nums[i] mod k, propagate E0 into E1 only for residues whose first occurrence is new since v was last seen. That version also passed all the random tests and ran in 0.25s, and it also uses only arrays. It is a two-state residue scan rather than a real dynamic-programming labelling, so I did not add dynamic-programming. The old summary was imperative ('Given ... find') and left out the k^2 residue-pair reduction that k <= 3000 enables, so I rewrote it. LeetCode's own topic tags may list Hash Table, but the technique doesn't need one.
